extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of early modern philosophy (Locke); philosophers and educated general readers
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Locke's criteria for when ideas are clear, distinct, real, fantastical, adequate or inadequate, and diagnosing sources of confusion arising from language, memory, or complexity. Useful for evaluating conceptual clarity and the reliability of ideas in argumentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Names as occasion of confusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Names, as supposed steady signs of things, and by their difference to stand for and keep things distinct, are the occasion of denominating ideas distinct or confused by a secret and unobserved reference the mind makes of its ideas to such names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To avoid confusion collect and unite into one complex idea, as precisely as possible, all ingredients that differentiate it, and apply steadily the same name. Be aware that loose application of names to undetermined or variable ideas covers ignorance and produces confusion (example: applying 'church' or 'idolatry' inconsistently).

rubrics_metrics.name: Confusion always concerns two ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Confusion consists in a difficulty to separate two things that should be separated; it always involves two ideas which approach one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an idea seems confused, examine which other idea it is in danger of being confounded with—often an idea belonging to another name. Determine whether the one is the same, a part of, or as properly called by the other name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of confused ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Confusion arises chiefly from loose application of names to undetermined, variable, or almost no ideas; complex ideas that memory cannot retain precisely; and failing to divine the precise complex idea a name stands for in another's use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevent confusion by making complex ideas more determinate in number and order of parts and by applying names steadily. Recognize that some confusion is not wilful but stems from complexity and memory limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex ideas may be distinct in one part and confused in another
rubrics_metrics.description: A compound idea can be very clear and distinct in one component yet obscure in another (example: the idea of a chiliaedron—number clear, figure unclear).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not infer full distinctness from a single clear element; when reasoning, mark which part of the complex idea your argument relies on and avoid drawing conclusions about the obscure parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confusion in argument when relying on obscure parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Using the familiar name for a whole complex idea that has obscure parts causes error in reasoning and dispute when deductions are drawn from those obscure parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test alleged distinctions by constructing near-cases (e.g., 999 vs. 1000 sides) to see whether the distinction is genuinely held in the relevant part. Keep reasoning confined to the parts you can distinctly conceive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas of infinity are confused and lead to error
rubrics_metrics.description: When discussing infinities (eternity, infinite divisibility), we lack a clear, positive idea of the whole extent; our ideas return to number and relative comparison, not a distinct conception of the actual infinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that arguments about actual infinite parts or eternity using such confused ideas will lead to blunders and absurdities; avoid treating additive or relative conceptions as if they were clear positive ideas of the infinite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple ideas are real appearances of things
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple ideas are effects of powers in things on our senses and so are real ideas that correspond to the real constitution or powers of things; the mind cannot invent simple ideas beyond what sensation supplies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat simple ideas (e.g., whiteness, coldness, pain) as adequate representations of the powers that produce them; they serve reliably as distinguishing characters even if they are not exact images of internal causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex ideas are voluntary combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex ideas are formed by the mind combining simple ideas under general names; these are not passively received but involve a measure of liberty in composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask which complex ideas correspond to reality and which are mere inventions; differences among people's complex ideas of the same term (e.g., gold, justice) often stem from different choices of included simple ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed modes and relations are real if consistent/possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixed modes and relations (complex ideas without reference to external archetypes) are real provided they are framed so as to be possible to exist; they are adequate to themselves because their archetype is the mind's own combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge such ideas by internal consistency and possibility of existence rather than by correspondence to external essences (example: courage as a complex idea of actions and states). Note that usage of established names can render such modes inadequate relative to others' patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex ideas of substances are real only when matching actual things
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex ideas intended to represent substances are real only insofar as their component simple ideas correspond to qualities that co-exist in actual substances; otherwise they are fantastical (examples: centaur, impossible mixtures of properties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deem a substance-idea fantastical when its constituent simple ideas have never been found united in any real thing or when they involve contradictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate vs inadequate ideas (definitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: ADEQUATE ideas perfectly represent their archetypes (what they are intended to stand for); INADEQUATE ideas are partial or incomplete representations of their archetypes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this distinction to assess whether an idea captures all features of its intended archetype; adequacy is relative to what the mind intends the idea to represent.

rubrics_metrics.name: All simple ideas are adequate
rubrics_metrics.description: Because simple ideas are immediate effects of powers in things and the mind cannot produce simple ideas by itself, all simple ideas are adequate—they correspond to the powers that produce them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat simple ideas as trustworthy matches to their causes (as far as sensation supplies them), even when folk language misattributes them as properties 'in' objects rather than powers producing ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes are adequate (but may be inadequate relative to settled names)
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex ideas of modes, being mind-made archetypes, are in themselves adequate, containing all the simple ideas the mind intends; however, when names are established by others, a person's mode-idea may be inadequate relative to that settled standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating someone's use of a term (e.g., 'courage'), check whether their internal complex idea corresponds to the community's established archetype; divergence makes their idea inadequate in the communicative sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas of substances referred to unknown real essences are inadequate
rubrics_metrics.description: When ideas of substances are referred to supposed real essences (unknown internal constitutions by which species are distinguished), our ideas are necessarily inadequate because we do not know those essences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical of treating species-names as standing for real essences; recognize that such reference renders our substance-ideas inadequate as representations of those essences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas of substances as collections of qualities are inadequate (inevitably partial)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when we build substance-ideas by collecting sensible qualities and powers we observe, these complex ideas omit innumerable other powers and properties; thus such ideas are still imperfect and inadequate representations of the substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume that listing a few salient properties (color, weight, hardness) captures the essence of a substance (example: gold has many properties beyond common lists). Acknowledge limitations of any such composite idea and avoid claiming demonstrative deductions about substance-essences from partial lists.
